description: We are building an interactive web tool for NASA’s SPHEREx mission: enter any sky coordinates (RA/Dec) and watch a time-lapse of infrared images to spot moving objects like brown dwarfs and comets. Planned features: spectra from the 102 bands, image differencing, and Gaia/WISE overlays. Our stack is Python (Astropy, FastAPI) and JavaScript. We’re looking for a frontend/UI developer and someone with astronomy or data-visualization experience
summary: SPHEREx Time-lapse Explorer is a free public web tool that lets anyone type a sky position (RA/Dec or an object name) and watch SPHEREx images of that spot as a short time-lapse video, so moving objects are easy to spot. For the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, we built a pipeline that queries IRSA (TAP, with SIA fallback) for every SPHEREx image covering the position, downloads only small cutouts, and reprojects them onto one common sky grid. In the browser, users can play the frames, stack them to reduce noise, subtract frames (minus median, minus previous, late half minus early half) to reveal movers, co-add per detector, and overlay Gaia DR3 sources moved to each frame's date using proper motion. A per-frame spectrum is also shown. We tested it on Barnard's Star, where the late-minus-early view shows its motion, and on R Dra. It matters because SPHEREx data is hard to explore without specialist tools; this makes it accessible to students and the public. Limits: faint objects such as WISE 0855 were not confirmed, and loading depends on IRSA availability.
details:
What it does

SPHEREx Time-lapse Explorer is a public web tool. The user enters a sky position (RA/Dec in degrees or sexagesimal, or an object name resolved through SIMBAD) and the tool plays every SPHEREx image covering that spot as a short time-lapse, so moving objects stand out between frames.

How it works

1. Find: the backend asks NASA/IPAC IRSA (TAP, with an SIA fallback) for all SPHEREx images covering the position. The query has no release filter, so new SPHEREx data appears automatically.

2. Cut out: only a small cutout of each image is downloaded through the IRSA cutout service and cached on disk.

3. Align: all cutouts are reprojected onto one common sky grid.

4. Explore: the browser plays the frames and offers stacking of N consecutive frames, frame minus median, frame minus previous, late half minus early half (to find movers), and co-add per detector (6 bands). Users can choose the detector (D1 to D6), field of view (0.5 to 60 arcmin), scale, colour map and contrast, and share a link to the exact view.

Extra features

- Gaia DR3 overlay: sources are moved to each frame's date using their proper motion, which also lets users check that frames are registered correctly.

- Per-frame spectrum: background-subtracted aperture brightness at the target for each frame, plotted against wavelength.

- Presets for test targets (Barnard's Star, WISE 0855, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aur, R Dra).

Benefits and impact

SPHEREx data normally needs specialist tools and archive knowledge. This tool lets students, teachers and the public explore the sky in the near-infrared and see motion and change with no installation, only a browser.

Tools

Python, FastAPI, Astropy, reproject, pyvo, NumPy; JavaScript, HTML and CSS canvas in the browser. Data: SPHEREx images from NASA/IPAC IRSA and Gaia DR3 from ESA.

Testing and limits

We tested it on Barnard's Star, where the late-minus-early view shows its motion as a light and dark pair, and on R Dra, found at its SIMBAD position. WISE 0855 was not confirmed because it was too faint in the frames we tried. The first load of a new position takes 30 to 120 seconds, and loading depends on IRSA availability: on 15 November 2026 IRSA's TAP service was temporarily down. The free hosting also sleeps when idle (about 50 seconds to wake).

AI assistance

Most of the code was generated by Claude (Anthropic), a generative AI assistant, under the team's direction. The team defined the goals, tested the tool on real SPHEREx and Gaia data, and decided on the changes.

This publication makes use of data products from SPHEREx, a joint project of JPL and Caltech funded by NASA.
